summary: Describes an optional method for encoding explicit sensitivity labels on IPv6 packets. It is meant only for multi-level secure networks that are both trusted and trustworthy. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: CALIPSO adds a label to each IPv6 packet that says how sensitive the packet's contents are. Routers and receiving computers use that label to decide whether the packet is allowed to travel on and who may receive it.

subtitle: Putting a security label on every IPv6 packet, so routers can enforce access rules.

tldr.problem: Networks that carry data at several levels of sensitivity need every packet to say how sensitive it is, so that routers and gateways can refuse to pass it to a system that is not cleared for it.
tldr.mechanism: CALIPSO defines an IPv6 hop-by-hop option that carries a domain of interpretation, a sensitivity level and a set of compartments, plus a checksum, and defines the checks that receiving systems and routers must apply.
tldr.outcome: The option is for closed, trusted multi-level secure networks only. The IESG note records that the IETF judged a hop-by-hop option acceptable for this one limited case and that the mechanism is unsuitable on the public Internet.

facts.label: Domains a node must support at once

today: RFC 5570 is an Informational memo published in July 2009, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It carries an IESG note that general deployment of hop-by-hop options is problematic, that a hop-by-hop option was judged acceptable for this one limited environment, and that the mechanism is unsuitable and ineffective on the global public Internet.

sections.title: Introduction and Intent
sections.content:
The original IPv4 specification included an option for labelling the sensitivity of IP packets, revised by RFC 1038 and later by RFC 1108. The IETF later deprecated RFC 1108, but that IPv4 option continues to be used inside a number of closed multi-level secure IP networks. One form of IP sensitivity label option or another has been in limited deployment for about two decades, usually in government or military internal networks, and there are commercial deployments where corporate security policies require mandatory access controls on sensitive data. Some banks use multi-level secure technology to restrict information about mergers and acquisitions.

CALIPSO specifies the equivalent explicit labelling for IPv6 packets. It is intended only for private internetworks that are disconnected from the global Internet, and the document says the option would not normally ever be visible in an IP packet on the public Internet. Because the consequences of a labeled packet escaping onto the public Internet would be severe, organisations deploying this mechanism have strong incentives to configure controls that prevent it, and a primary purpose of the mechanism is to enable deployment of mandatory access controls for IPv6 packets. An open specification is nevertheless needed so that end systems and routers inside such a deployment interoperate.

The document records why the IPv4 option exists and why the IPv6 form is simpler. The IPv4 option was designed for one device, an IPv4 packet-encryption device called a BLACKER, and the limited space in IPv4 headers led to one non-IETF specification having many sub-options, which made it much harder for routers and guard systems to enforce access controls at wire speed. Ethernet link speeds have risen from 10 Mbps half duplex to 10 Gbps full duplex and beyond, and forwarding at those speeds needs support from dedicated chips, so a single simple option format matters more than ever. The document notes that a node must be able to support at least two domains of interpretation concurrently, because a deployment cannot otherwise migrate from one domain to another without downtime.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks carry data at more than one level of secrecy, and the rules say a packet may only travel on links cleared for its level. To enforce that, every packet has to carry its level. CALIPSO defines that field for IPv6.

sections.title: Domains, Levels and Compartments
sections.content:
A domain of interpretation is a way of identifying the labelling, classification and handling system in use for a particular set of data, the systems and people that process it, and the networks that carry it. A label of SECRET by itself is meaningless; one also has to know which organisation it belongs to before deciding who may receive the data. A CALIPSO domain is an opaque identifier pointing at a set of policies that define the levels and compartments within it. The scope of a domain depends on the organisation that creates it: a multinational organisation such as NATO might create one that member nations then use.

A sensitivity level represents mandatory separation of data by relative sensitivity, and levels always have a specific ordering within a domain. Clearance to access one level implies access to all the less sensitive ones. Common United Kingdom terms, from low to high, are UNCLASSIFIED, RESTRICTED, CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET and MOST SECRET. A compartment represents mandatory segregation by formal information category or access programme, such as the FINANCE and R&D compartments of a small company. Each compartment is separate and distinct, and access to one gives no access to another.

The document also describes how releasabilities are carried: a releasability is encoded on the wire as if it were an inverted compartment, because operating systems in multi-level secure environments do not support releasabilities as a concept separate from compartments.

Together, a domain, a level and a set of compartments form a sensitivity label. The verb dominate describes a comparison between two labels in the same domain: label A dominates label B if A's level is greater than or equal to B's level and A's compartment set is a superset of B's. Labels from different domains cannot be compared this way at all.
sections.plainLanguage: A label has three parts. The domain says whose rules apply. The level says how sensitive the data is, and levels are ordered within a domain. The compartments say which groups the data belongs to, so that two teams can each handle only their own.

sections.title: Architecture and the Access Control Model
sections.content:
CALIPSO describes a convention for labelling an IPv6 datagram within a particular system security policy, designed for use inside a mandatory access control system. It builds on the formal Bell-LaPadula model, which has two principles. No write down: an entity at a minimum level must not be able to write information marked below that level. No read up: an entity at a maximum level must not be able to read information above that level. In a normal deployment, downgrading must not happen automatically; it is permitted only when a person with the right privilege manually checks that the information may be downgraded and relabels it. The document extends this model to separate domains of interpretation, each of which is a single comparable domain of labels.

The specification is focused on two things: how to encode sensitivity labels in packets, and how routers and end systems are to interpret and enforce them at the IP layer. It does not cover how the network label is enforced inside an end system once a packet is accepted, which is out of scope for a network-layer encoding standard. Each distinct sensitivity label represents a separate virtual network sharing the same physical network, and nodes that implement the protocol must enforce that separation.

The specification does not enable automatic relabelling, either within a domain or between domains. Implementers must not permit automatic upgrading or downgrading in the default configuration; a configuration knob may be provided for a system security officer with the right privilege, but the default setting must be that automatic upgrading and downgrading are disabled.

Each physical interface of a node is associated with one or more sensitivity label ranges, and ranges from different domains are enumerated separately. Each logical interface also has ranges, and every range on a logical interface must fall within a range defined for the corresponding physical interface. When data leaves an end system it is exported to the network, marked with a domain, level and compartment set derived from its internal label and the export domain. When data arrives it is imported, and the received label becomes the internal label of the data, assuming the domain is recognised and the datagram is within range for the receiving interface. In transit, a datagram is handled on the basis of its label and is usually neither imported nor exported by the intermediate systems it passes through. The document also describes CALIPSO gateways, which import data from one domain and export it to another so that the effective label does not change but is represented with a different domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are the classic ones: information must not flow downwards to a system that is not cleared for it, and a system must not read information above its own level. A router enforces this by checking each packet's label against the range allowed on the link it is about to use.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
CALIPSO is an IPv6 hop-by-hop option rather than a destination option, so that a security gateway or router can apply access controls to a packet based on the label it carries. The option data must not change en route, except when a trusted intermediate system performs a domain translation, when a trusted intermediate system inserts a label into an unlabelled packet, or when a last-hop trusted system removes a label before forwarding to a destination that does not support labels. A node that does not recognise the option must ignore it, but every implementation of this specification must recognise it and must not ignore it.

The option type field holds the unsigned 8-bit value 00000111, that is, the option number 7 registered with IANA. The option length field is one octet with a minimum value of eight, and it gives the length of the option data in octets, excluding the type and length fields themselves. The domain of interpretation field is an unsigned 32-bit integer, with IANA maintaining a registry of the values used in it. The null domain, in which all four octets are zero, must never appear on the wire: a packet carrying it must be dropped and the event logged as a security fault.

The sensitivity level field is an unsigned 8-bit value whose ordering must be respected, with 00000000 the lowest level and 11111111 the highest, so that routers can apply policy with minimal per-packet computation and minimal configuration. The compartment length field is an unsigned 8-bit integer giving the size of the compartment bitmap in 32-bit words, with a minimum of zero used when the information in the packet is in no compartment at all. The checksum field is 16 bits and holds a CRC-16 checksum as defined in Appendix C of RFC 1662, calculated over the whole option including its header with the checksum field zeroed. It must always be computed on transmission and always verified on reception, and it is required even when other integrity protection such as the authentication header is in use.

The compartment bitmap holds a variable number of 64-bit words, one bit per compartment in the domain, where a set bit means the packet's data must be protected under that compartment's rules. Which bit means which compartment is left to the owner of the domain. Because releasabilities are carried as inverted compartments, the bitmap holds both the logical compartments and the logical releasabilities for the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is a short header added to the packet. It names the domain, gives the level as a number, lists the compartments as a set of bits, and carries a checksum so that a corrupted label is caught before it is acted on.

sections.title: Processing by End Systems, Routers and Gateways
sections.content:
Each node evaluates the label on an arriving packet, checks that it is valid for the receiving interface, and at a minimum forwards the packet only to an interface and node whose range includes the packet's label. Packets with an invalid or out-of-range label must be dropped on receipt, and these rules apply at every hop a labeled packet traverses, not only at the ends of a session. It is a violation of the default policy for a packet marked MOST SECRET to transit a link whose maximum level is SECRET. A label is valid only if it falls within the range of the sending interface on the sending system and the range of the receiving interface on the receiving system.

An end system exporting data selects an export domain in a defined order: the domain chosen by the upper-layer protocol if there is one, otherwise a default domain defined for the destination address or network, otherwise a domain associated with the sending logical interface, otherwise the system default. A connection-oriented session must keep the same domain and label for its whole life, and the domain is selected when the connection is initiated. Once the domain is selected, the label and its values are derived from the internal label; if the internal level does not map to a valid label in that domain, an error should be returned to the upper-layer protocol and no further attempt to send the datagram should be made. Finally the packet's label is compared with the range associated with the chosen logical interface, and the packet is only sent if that interface permits the domain and the label is within range for it.

On import, the receiving end system verifies the checksum and silently drops a packet that fails it, verifies that the domain is known and valid, verifies that the domain is permitted on the receiving interface, and verifies that the label is within the permitted range for that interface. Each permitted domain on an interface has its own range table. A packet whose label is disjoint from the range, below it or above it must be dropped, and no ICMP error message may be sent in these cases. Once accepted, the import label and domain are used to associate the right internal label with the data, and that information is passed up to the upper layer.

An intermediate system applies the same input checks before anything else: whether the datagram is addressed to it, in which case it acts as an end system, then the checksum, the domain validity, the domain permission and the range. Only if all of those pass is the packet forwarded. On output, the system checks that the packet carries a label if the output interface requires one, that the domain is permitted on the sending interface, and that the label is within range there; packets that fail are dropped, and an ICMP destination unreachable message may follow, with the reason code No Route to Host for an unrecognised or prohibited domain and Administratively Prohibited for a valid domain with an out-of-range label or a missing required label. Any error message is sent with the same label as the packet that caused it.

A system that relabels on the fly does so after the input checks and before the output checks. It can either convert the label to an internal label and back, which is the same as importing and exporting, or map one CALIPSO label directly onto another. The output domain may be chosen from the incoming domain, the incoming label, the destination system, network, subnetwork, the sending interface or the receiving interface. The mapping must be consistent and reversible: if a packet from A to B with domain X maps into domain Y, then a packet from B to A with domain Y should map back into domain X. If the input label does not map to a valid output label, the packet is silently dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router checks a packet's label against the range allowed on the link it arrived on, and again on the link it is about to use. A packet that fails either check is dropped without an error message, so that nothing is revealed about why it was refused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Correct implementation of this mechanism is critical to the security of the systems and networks where it is deployed, and the use of high-assurance development techniques is encouraged.

Because the label is used to make access control decisions, some way of binding the label to the rest of the packet is needed. Without it, a malicious change to the label would go undetected. Implementations must therefore also support the IP Authentication Header, and must let the system administrator configure whether it is used. ESP with null encryption cannot protect hop-by-hop options, whereas the authentication header protects all invariant headers and data of an IPv6 packet, including the CALIPSO option.

If a labelled IP security association is used within a deployment, the sensitivity label of that association must have the same meaning as the label carried in the packet, so that access control policy is applied correctly. Because the authentication header includes the CALIPSO option among the protected fields, a modified packet fails authentication at the destination, so labels cannot be inserted, deleted or translated in packets that carry an authentication header. Where policy requires a modification that the authentication header forbids, the packet must be dropped instead, and an ICMP destination unreachable message with the reason code Administratively Prohibited should be sent.

The mechanism is only intended for very limited circumstances, in a well-protected operating environment where the risk of attack is acceptable to the accreditor of the systems involved. Packets carrying visible labels ought never to traverse the public Internet, although subject to local policy they may cross it with suitable cryptographic protection, for example through a tunnel-mode ESP VPN or over a link protected by certified bulk encryptors. The specification does not seek to eliminate every covert channel, and the accreditor should consider personnel clearances, physical security, and electronic, network and communications security as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The label itself has to be protected, or someone could change it to gain access. The authentication header does that, and it also means a labelled packet cannot have its label changed in flight: such a packet is dropped instead.

items.title: Domain of interpretation
items.text: An identifier for the set of policies that define the levels and compartments in use.

items.title: Sensitivity level
items.text: An ordered number: clearance for one level implies clearance for all lower ones.

items.title: Compartment set
items.text: The groups the data belongs to, carried as a set of bits, one bit per compartment.

items.title: Releasability
items.text: Carried on the wire as if it were an inverted compartment.
